purpose: Machine-readable conceptual-computing-literacy ontology of evaluable explanatory/decision work-units that let a non-specialist reason correctly about how computers actually work (hardware and data representation: binary/bits/bytes/encodings, CPU execution, memory hierarchy, storage; software layers: operating systems, processes/threads, compilers vs interpreters, networking; algorithms and data structures: arrays, hash maps, trees, sorting/searching; and complexity: Big-O, tractability, recursion, time/space tradeoffs), oriented to understanding rather than building, as a subdomain node of Computing & How LLMs Work (Foundations) within a knowledge-searcher meta-KB that routes each concept to authoritative sources, verifies explanations against them, and synthesizes one coherent layered mental model.
assumptions: Scope is conceptual computing literacy for understanding how computers work, not a build/engineering guide.
No observed dataset or benchmark evidence supplied; all numeric values are heuristic priors.
Nodes are evaluable explanatory/decision work-units that let a non-specialist reason correctly about computing systems.
The parent domain is Computing & How LLMs Work (Foundations); this KB models the computing_and_systems_fundamentals subdomain.
As a knowledge-searcher node, explanatory work-units are paired with routing each concept to authoritative sources and verifying claims against them.
Coverage spans hardware/data representation, software layers, algorithms/data structures, and complexity at a literacy depth.
exclusions: Hands-on build guides, production engineering, performance tuning, and vendor-specific configuration.
Deep formal treatments (microarchitecture, optimizing-compiler internals, complexity proofs) beyond literacy framing.
Programming-language syntax tutorials and coding instruction.
Hardware design, electronics, and chip fabrication detail.
LLM internals proper, which belong to sibling subdomains of the parent domain.

competency_questions.question: Which abstraction layer and goal does a given computing question belong to, and what is the success criterion for understanding it?
How does a concept connect down to its mechanism and up to its use across abstraction layers?
How do computers represent numbers, bits, bytes, and text, why do width and encoding matter, and why is bytes-vs-characters real?
What does it physically mean to 'run code', and why does memory access cost vary by orders of magnitude?
What is the difference between memory and storage, and what survives power loss?
What does the operating system do between programs and hardware, and how do processes/threads relate?
How does human-written source become machine actions, and why is concurrent code hard?
How does data move across a network from a request to a response?
Why are some data-structure operations cheap and others expensive (arrays, hash maps)?
When do logarithmic structures and the right search/sort choice change runtime, and what are their preconditions?
How do we compare algorithms by how they scale rather than by constant factors?
Which problems are tractable vs intractable, and how do recursion and Big-O frame scaling?
How can memory be traded for speed (or vice versa), and when does recursion's stack cost matter?
How is each concept routed to an authoritative source, verified against it free of myths, and synthesized into one coherent layer-ordered mental model with a reusable handoff artifact?

glossary.definition: the smallest unit of information, a single binary 0 or 1
a group of (usually) eight bits, the common unit of addressable memory
a scheme mapping characters or data to byte sequences (e.g. UTF-8)
a small fast memory tier that holds recently or likely-used data to cut access latency
an OS-managed running program with its own isolated address space
a unit of execution within a process that shares the process address space
translating source code ahead of time into machine code or bytecode
a discrete unit of data sent across a network with addressing metadata
a structure giving amortized O(1) keyed lookup via a hash function into buckets
notation describing how an algorithm's cost grows with input size, ignoring constants
defining a solution in terms of smaller instances of itself with a base case
solvable in polynomial time, i.e. with an efficient known algorithm
a level of the computing stack that hides lower-level detail from the level above

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established computing-literacy and systems literature (Petzold, Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software; Bryant & O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective) and standard CS-education practice; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Frame the learner's question into the layered mental model (hardware->data->software->network->algorithms->complexity) so the right explanatory work-units and sources are selected.
contradictors: explainer who jumps to jargon without placing the concept in a layer

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect scope_and_mental_model

pros.claim: everything downstream inherits which layer and source set the concept belongs to
pros.example: placing 'why is my program slow' at the complexity+memory layers, not the syntax layer

cons.claim: over-scoping turns one question into a whole course and stalls the explanation
cons.example: treating 'what is a byte' as requiring full CPU microarchitecture

failure_modes: goal misread as build-guide when only understanding is needed
acceptance_tests: the chosen layer answers the actual question asked
a non-specialist can restate the concept's place in the stack
scope excludes build-guide work when goal is understanding
revisit_triggers: goal shifts from understand to build

nodes.definition: Explain how computers represent integers and other values in binary (and hex/octal) and convert between bases so a non-specialist can read and reason about machine numbers.
contradictors: intuition that 'numbers are just numbers' ignoring fixed width

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect number_systems_and_binary

pros.claim: grounds every higher concept: encodings, addresses, and data sizes all reduce to binary
pros.example: explaining why 255+1 wraps to 0 in an 8-bit unsigned byte

cons.claim: base arithmetic feels abstract and learners memorize tricks without the positional model
cons.example: reciting a hex table without understanding place value

failure_modes: ignoring fixed width causing silent overflow
acceptance_tests: learner converts a value across binary/decimal/hex correctly
learner predicts overflow at a given width

nodes.definition: Explain bits, bytes, words, and how text and other data are encoded (ASCII, Unicode/UTF-8) so a non-specialist understands how meaning maps onto bytes.
contradictors: belief that one character always equals one byte
inputs: a 'why is this text garbled' or 'how big is this data' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect bits_bytes_and_encodings

pros.claim: explains real failures like mojibake and size budgeting that non-specialists hit daily
pros.example: diagnosing garbled text as a UTF-8-read-as-Latin-1 encoding mismatch

cons.claim: the bytes-vs-characters distinction is subtle and easy to state but hard to internalize
cons.example: assuming a 10-character emoji string is 10 bytes

acceptance_tests: learner explains why a multibyte character is not one byte
learner identifies an encoding-mismatch cause of garbled text

nodes.definition: Explain how a CPU fetches, decodes, and executes instructions (fetch-decode-execute, registers, clock, basic pipelining) so a non-specialist understands what 'running code' physically means.
contradictors: mental model where the CPU 'reads the source code directly'
inputs: a 'how does code actually run' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect cpu_and_instruction_execution

pros.claim: demystifies 'running' as concrete instruction stepping over registers and memory
pros.example: showing a loop as repeated fetch-decode-execute over a counter register

cons.claim: real CPUs add pipelining/out-of-order that can mislead if over-simplified or over-detailed
cons.example: explaining branch prediction before the basic cycle is understood

failure_modes: treating CPU as executing source directly
ignoring registers vs memory speed gap
acceptance_tests: learner describes the fetch-decode-execute loop
learner distinguishes a register from main memory

nodes.definition: Explain the memory hierarchy (registers, cache levels, RAM, disk) and locality/caching so a non-specialist can reason about why memory access cost varies by orders of magnitude.
contradictors: model where 'all memory is equally fast'
inputs: a 'why is this slow / why does layout matter' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect memory_hierarchy_and_caching

pros.claim: explains huge real-world speed differences from layout and access patterns
pros.example: row-major array traversal being far faster than column-major due to locality

cons.claim: the orders-of-magnitude latency table is easy to recite but its consequences are subtle
cons.example: quoting cache latencies without connecting them to access patterns

failure_modes: ignoring locality when reasoning about speed
acceptance_tests: learner ranks register/cache/RAM/disk by latency
learner predicts which access pattern is cache-friendly
revisit_triggers: new storage tier or accelerator memory introduced

nodes.definition: Explain persistent storage (HDD/SSD, files, blocks, volatile vs non-volatile) so a non-specialist understands the difference between memory and storage and what survives power loss.

included: durability and the cost of writes

contradictors: belief that 'saving' and 'being in memory' are the same
inputs: a 'what survives a reboot / memory vs disk' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect storage_and_persistence

pros.claim: clears a common confusion that blocks reasoning about state, files, and reboots
pros.example: explaining why unsaved RAM data is lost on power failure but a saved file is not

cons.claim: the memory/storage boundary blurs with caching, mmap, and swap
cons.example: conflating OS page cache with durable disk writes

acceptance_tests: learner states what is lost on power loss
learner compares SSD and HDD on a relevant tradeoff

nodes.definition: Explain what an operating system does (kernel, system calls, resource management, virtual memory, the abstraction it provides over hardware) so a non-specialist understands the layer between programs and hardware.
contradictors: model where applications talk to hardware directly
inputs: a 'what does the OS actually do' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect operating_system_abstractions

pros.claim: the OS is the hinge concept linking hardware to all running software and isolation
pros.example: explaining why one crashed app does not take down the whole machine via process isolation

cons.claim: the OS surface is huge and easy to over-scope into a full course
cons.example: diving into scheduler classes before the user/kernel boundary is clear

failure_modes: treating virtual memory as physical memory
acceptance_tests: learner explains why a program uses system calls for I/O
learner describes how virtual memory isolates processes

nodes.definition: Explain processes vs threads, concurrency vs parallelism, and basic synchronization hazards so a non-specialist can reason about why concurrent programs are hard.

included: process vs thread and address-space sharing
race conditions and deadlock at a conceptual level

contradictors: belief that adding threads always makes a program faster
inputs: a 'why is concurrent code buggy / why not just add threads' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect processes_threads_concurrency

pros.claim: explains a major class of real bugs and why parallel speedup is bounded
pros.example: showing a lost-update race when two threads increment a shared counter without a lock

cons.claim: subtle nondeterminism makes intuition unreliable and over-claims dangerous
cons.example: assuming a race 'works' because it passed once

acceptance_tests: learner distinguishes a process from a thread
learner identifies a race condition in a simple example

nodes.definition: Explain the path from source code to execution (compilation, interpretation, bytecode/VMs, JIT) so a non-specialist understands how human-written code becomes machine actions.
contradictors: belief that all languages 'run the same way'
inputs: a 'how does my code become something the CPU runs' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect compilers_vs_interpreters

pros.claim: connects the human-readable source layer to actual CPU execution
pros.example: explaining why a compiled binary runs without the source but a script needs an interpreter

cons.claim: modern hybrids (bytecode+JIT) blur the compiled/interpreted line and confuse simple framings
cons.example: calling a JIT language 'interpreted' and missing why it gets fast

failure_modes: treating compiled vs interpreted as a hard binary
acceptance_tests: learner explains why compiled code does not ship source
learner places bytecode/JIT between compile and interpret

nodes.definition: Explain how data moves across a network (packets, layered model, IP addresses, TCP/UDP, DNS, client-server and request-response) so a non-specialist can reason about what happens when they load a page.

included: IP addressing and routing at a conceptual level

contradictors: model where data travels as one continuous stream over a single wire
inputs: a 'what happens when I load a website / how does data get there' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect networking_how_data_moves

pros.claim: turns the opaque 'internet' into a traceable chain of name lookup, packets, and layers
pros.example: walking a URL load from DNS lookup to TCP connection to HTTP response

cons.claim: the full stack has many layers; over-detailing buries the core request-response intuition
cons.example: teaching all OSI layers before the client-server idea lands

failure_modes: ignoring layering and treating the network as a single hop
acceptance_tests: learner traces a web request from DNS to response
learner picks TCP vs UDP for a given need

nodes.definition: Explain arrays and contiguous-memory structures, indexing, and their access/insert tradeoffs so a non-specialist can reason about why some operations are cheap and others expensive.
contradictors: belief that all collection operations cost the same
inputs: a 'why is indexing fast but inserting slow' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect arrays_and_contiguous_memory

pros.claim: connects a concrete structure to both Big-O and cache behavior
pros.example: explaining O(1) random access and why mid-array insertion is O(n)

cons.claim: learners overgeneralize array tradeoffs to all structures
cons.example: assuming a hash map also has O(1) indexing by position

acceptance_tests: learner gives the cost of index access vs mid-insert
learner explains why arrays are cache-friendly

nodes.definition: Explain hash maps/dictionaries, hashing, collisions, and amortized O(1) lookup so a non-specialist can reason about when constant-time keyed access applies and when it degrades.

included: collision handling at a conceptual level

contradictors: belief that hash-map lookup is always exactly O(1)
inputs: a 'why is dictionary lookup fast (usually)' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect hash_maps_and_hashing

pros.claim: explains the workhorse structure behind fast keyed lookup in almost every program
pros.example: explaining why a set membership check is near-instant regardless of size

cons.claim: the average-vs-worst-case distinction is subtle and the 'always O(1)' myth is sticky
cons.example: claiming O(1) while ignoring adversarial collisions degrading to O(n)

failure_modes: ignoring hash quality and load factor
acceptance_tests: learner explains collisions and amortized O(1)
learner identifies a worst-case degradation cause

nodes.definition: Explain trees (binary trees, BSTs, balanced trees, tries) and hierarchical organization so a non-specialist can reason about logarithmic operations and why structure shape matters.

included: BST ordering and O(log n) operations

contradictors: belief that trees are always logarithmic regardless of shape
inputs: a 'why are sorted/searchable structures O(log n)' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect trees_and_hierarchical_structures

pros.claim: explains ordered, searchable structure underlying indexes and sorted data
pros.example: explaining why a balanced BST finds an item in O(log n) by halving the search each step

cons.claim: unbalanced trees degrade to O(n); the balancing caveat is easy to omit
cons.example: presenting a BST as O(log n) while a degenerate insert order makes it O(n)

failure_modes: ignoring balancing and assuming log time
confusing tree traversal order with search
acceptance_tests: learner explains why a balanced tree is O(log n)
learner names a case where a tree degrades to O(n)

nodes.definition: Explain core sorting and searching algorithms and their cost classes so a non-specialist can reason about why algorithm choice changes runtime by orders of magnitude.

included: linear vs binary search and the sorted precondition
comparison sorts and O(n log n) bound

contradictors: belief that sorting/searching choice rarely matters
inputs: a 'which algorithm and why' question over ordered data

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect sorting_and_searching

pros.claim: makes the practical payoff of complexity concrete via search/sort choices
pros.example: explaining why binary search beats linear scan on large sorted data

cons.claim: the sorted precondition for binary search is routinely forgotten
cons.example: applying binary search to unsorted data and getting wrong results

failure_modes: using binary search on unsorted data
ignoring the n log n lower bound for comparison sorts
acceptance_tests: learner states binary search's precondition
learner gives the cost class of a comparison sort

nodes.definition: Explain Big-O notation and asymptotic time/space analysis so a non-specialist can compare algorithms by how they scale rather than by constant-factor detail.

included: common classes O(1),O(log n),O(n),O(n log n),O(n^2),O(2^n)

contradictors: belief that constant factors or micro-benchmarks settle scaling questions
inputs: a 'how does this scale / which is faster for large n' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect big_o_and_asymptotic_analysis

pros.claim: the shared vocabulary that lets any two algorithms be compared by scaling
pros.example: explaining why O(n log n) sorting beats O(n^2) sorting as input grows large

cons.claim: learners conflate Big-O with real wall-clock time and ignore constants that matter at small n
cons.example: claiming an O(log n) method is always faster than O(n) even for tiny inputs

failure_modes: confusing asymptotic class with real runtime
acceptance_tests: learner orders common complexity classes by growth
learner explains why constants are dropped

nodes.definition: Explain tractable vs intractable problems (polynomial vs exponential, the practical meaning of NP-hardness) so a non-specialist can recognize when a problem has no known efficient exact solution.

included: P vs NP at a literacy level

contradictors: belief that more compute will eventually brute-force any problem cheaply
inputs: a 'why can't this just be computed exactly/fast' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect tractability_and_intractability

pros.claim: sets realistic expectations about what computation can and cannot do efficiently
pros.example: explaining why exact route optimization over many cities is infeasible and heuristics are used

cons.claim: the literacy framing risks overclaiming about P vs NP, which is unresolved
cons.example: stating NP-hard problems are 'impossible' rather than 'no known efficient exact solution'

failure_modes: overstating settled facts about P vs NP
acceptance_tests: learner distinguishes polynomial from exponential scaling
learner explains why heuristics are used for intractable problems

nodes.definition: Explain recursion (base case, recursive case, the call stack, and recursion vs iteration) so a non-specialist can read and reason about self-referential algorithms.

included: the call stack and stack growth

contradictors: belief that recursion is just a stylistic alternative with no cost model
inputs: a 'how does a function that calls itself work / why does it overflow' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect recursion_and_self_reference

pros.claim: unlocks divide-and-conquer algorithms and explains a common crash class
pros.example: explaining why missing a base case causes a stack-overflow via unbounded call-stack growth

cons.claim: learners fear recursion or misjudge its stack cost vs iteration
cons.example: rewriting an iterative loop as deep recursion and exhausting the stack

acceptance_tests: learner identifies the base case in a recursive example
learner explains why deep recursion can overflow the stack

nodes.definition: Explain time/space tradeoffs (caching, memoization, precomputation vs recomputation) so a non-specialist can reason about exchanging memory for speed and vice versa.
contradictors: belief that an algorithm can be made both minimal time and minimal space for free
inputs: a 'can I trade memory for speed here' question

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect time_space_tradeoffs

pros.claim: frames a recurring engineering decision in literacy terms
pros.example: explaining why memoizing repeated computations trades memory to cut time

cons.claim: not every problem has a useful tradeoff and naive caching can hurt
cons.example: caching results that are never reused and wasting memory

failure_modes: caching without considering reuse or staleness
acceptance_tests: learner gives an example of trading space for time
learner identifies when memoization helps

nodes.definition: Map any computing concept to its abstraction layer and to the adjacent layers it depends on, so explanations stay at the right level and connect down to mechanism and up to use.
contradictors: explainer who stays at one layer and never connects up or down
inputs: a scoped concept and its target layer

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect abstraction_layer_mapping

pros.claim: keeps explanations at the right altitude and prevents both hand-waving and rabbit-holing
pros.example: linking 'why is my loop slow' down to memory hierarchy and up to Big-O

cons.claim: over-linking layers can overwhelm a non-specialist with irrelevant depth
cons.example: explaining cache lines when the learner only needed the loop's Big-O

acceptance_tests: the explanation sits at the layer the question targets
each concept links to at least one adjacent layer when relevant
revisit_triggers: new layer or concept area added to scope

nodes.definition: Route each computing concept to authoritative explanatory sources (foundational books, standards, reference docs) and select the right one for the learner's depth and goal.

included: Petzold for ground-up intuition, Bryant & O'Hallaron for systems depth

contradictors: explainer who cites nothing or routes every question to one generic web search
inputs: a scoped concept and learner depth/goal

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect concept_to_source_routing

pros.claim: ties the literacy KB to where authoritative answers actually live, fitting the knowledge-searcher role
pros.example: routing a 'how does code reach the CPU' question to Petzold for intuition and B&O for depth

cons.claim: source authority and freshness vary; routing can mislead if currency is ignored
cons.example: citing an outdated edition for a topic where details changed

failure_modes: routing to an unauthoritative or stale source
mismatching source depth to learner level
acceptance_tests: each concept maps to at least one named authoritative source
source depth matches the learner's stated goal
revisit_triggers: new authoritative source or edition becomes available

nodes.definition: Verify that an explanation is technically correct, not over-claimed, and free of common myths before it is delivered, so a non-specialist is not taught a wrong mental model.

included: myth detection (e.g. 1 char = 1 byte, hash always O(1))

contradictors: explainer who ships confident but subtly wrong analogies
inputs: a drafted explanation and its source routing

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect explanation_correctness_verification

pros.claim: prevents propagating durable misconceptions that are hard to unlearn
pros.example: catching and correcting an 'a hash map is always O(1)' claim before delivery

cons.claim: verification adds latency and can over-hedge into uselessly qualified answers
cons.example: burying a correct simple answer under excessive caveats

failure_modes: shipping a plausible but wrong analogy
over-hedging until the answer is unusable
acceptance_tests: each delivered claim is checkable against a source
known myths in the topic are explicitly addressed
over-claims are flagged or removed

nodes.definition: Synthesize verified work-units into a coherent, layer-ordered explanation with a reusable handoff artifact so the learner gets one correct mental model rather than disconnected facts.

included: narrative that links mechanism to use

contradictors: explainer who dumps disconnected facts without a through-line

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new sources, corrections, or scope changes affect synthesis_and_handoff

pros.claim: delivers the single coherent mental model that was the whole point, with reuse for next questions
pros.example: assembling binary->encoding->memory into one story for 'why is my text data so big'

cons.claim: premature synthesis before verification ships a polished but wrong narrative
cons.example: writing a clean explanation that still contains an unverified myth

failure_modes: losing the layer through-line in assembly
acceptance_tests: the explanation is ordered by abstraction layer
the handoff artifact lists concepts, sources, and caveats
the acceptance criterion for 'understood' is met
revisit_triggers: learner reports the model did not click

edges.why_related: scope selects the data-representation layer before binary is explained
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining binary when the question was about networking
edges.example: 'why is text big' scoped to encoding not ALU design

edges.why_related: layer mapping requires the scoped concept and goal
edges.risk_of_conflict: mapping layers for an unscoped question
edges.example: placing 'slow loop' before mapping its layers
edges.resolution_rule: scope the concept before mapping layers

edges.why_related: complexity questions must be scoped to the scaling layer first
edges.benefit_of_coupling: keeps Big-O tied to the actual question
edges.risk_of_conflict: jumping to Big-O for a hardware question
edges.example: scoping 'why slow' to complexity vs memory

edges.why_related: encodings are built on binary integer representation
edges.risk_of_conflict: teaching UTF-8 before binary place value
edges.example: explaining code points as binary before bytes

edges.why_related: instructions and registers hold binary values
edges.benefit_of_coupling: binary grounds what the CPU manipulates
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining registers without binary values
edges.example: showing a counter register as a binary value

edges.why_related: the memory hierarchy explains where CPU operands come from and their cost
edges.risk_of_conflict: discussing cache before the fetch cycle
edges.example: fetch stalls explained via cache miss

edges.why_related: storage is the slowest, persistent tier of the hierarchy
edges.benefit_of_coupling: frames volatility against the latency ladder
edges.risk_of_conflict: teaching disk durability without the latency context
edges.example: placing disk at the bottom of the latency ladder

edges.why_related: the OS schedules execution onto the CPU and mediates hardware
edges.benefit_of_coupling: execution model grounds what the OS manages
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining scheduling before the execution cycle
edges.example: OS time-slicing shown over the fetch cycle

edges.why_related: virtual memory is an OS abstraction over the memory hierarchy
edges.risk_of_conflict: teaching virtual memory without the physical hierarchy
edges.example: mapping virtual pages onto RAM and disk

edges.why_related: processes and threads are OS-managed units of execution
edges.benefit_of_coupling: OS context grounds isolation and scheduling
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining threads without the OS boundary
edges.example: process isolation explained via OS address spaces

edges.why_related: the OS provides the network stack and sockets programs use
edges.benefit_of_coupling: OS layer grounds where networking sits
edges.risk_of_conflict: teaching packets without the host's role
edges.example: sockets shown as an OS service

edges.why_related: compilation/interpretation targets the CPU's instruction execution
edges.benefit_of_coupling: execution model grounds the translation target
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining compilers without what they target
edges.example: compiled binary mapped to fetch-decode-execute

edges.why_related: contiguous arrays' cache-friendliness comes from the memory hierarchy
edges.benefit_of_coupling: memory model explains array access cost
edges.risk_of_conflict: claiming array speed without locality
edges.example: sequential array scan as cache-friendly

edges.why_related: hash maps are typically backed by arrays of buckets
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining buckets without the array backing
edges.example: buckets as an array indexed by hash

edges.why_related: trees contrast with contiguous arrays in layout and cost
edges.risk_of_conflict: teaching trees without the array contrast

edges.why_related: sort/search algorithm comparison uses Big-O classes
edges.risk_of_conflict: comparing sorts without complexity classes
edges.example: binary vs linear search compared by Big-O

edges.why_related: sorting and searching operate over array-backed sequences
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining binary search without indexed access
edges.example: binary search using O(1) array indexing

edges.why_related: after scoping, encoding questions follow data-representation framing
edges.benefit_of_coupling: keeps encoding work in the right phase
edges.risk_of_conflict: explaining encodings before scoping the question
edges.example: sequencing encoding after layer placement

edges.why_related: tractability is framed in terms of polynomial vs exponential Big-O classes

edges.why_related: verification can flag P-vs-NP over-claims and trigger revisit of the tractability framing

edges.risk_of_conflict: claiming NP-hard means impossible

edges.resolution_rule: revisit framing; stop when claim is correctly hedged and re-verified

edges.why_related: simple byte-size intuition tension with compression/encoding choices that trade space

edges.why_related: cache-friendly contiguous layout conflicts with cheap insertion/deletion needs
edges.risk_of_conflict: picking arrays for an insert-heavy workload for cache reasons

edges.why_related: hash maps (avg O(1), unordered) conflict with trees (O(log n), ordered) for the same lookup need

edges.example: hash map vs balanced BST for range queries
edges.resolution_rule: pick by ordering and worst-case needs; explain why

edges.why_related: asymptotic class can mislead vs real wall-clock driven by constants and hardware
edges.risk_of_conflict: calling O(log n) always faster than O(n) at tiny n
edges.example: constant factors dominating at small input
edges.resolution_rule: use Big-O for scaling, measure for small n; state the regime

edges.why_related: thorough verification adds latency tension with delivering a timely synthesis
edges.risk_of_conflict: shipping fast but unverified, or stalling on over-verification
edges.example: delaying an answer for low-value extra checks
edges.resolution_rule: verify load-bearing claims first; deliver with explicit residual caveats

edges.why_related: sources should be routed before the final synthesis cites them

conflict_axes.trigger: adding rigorous detail risks losing the non-specialist learner
resolution_order: fix the target altitude from the goal
add depth only where it changes the answer
offer optional deeper sources
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for an understanding goal accessibility dominates; add depth only when it materially changes correctness
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if accuracy cannot be preserved at the chosen altitude
conflict_axes.example: explaining pipelining detail when the learner only needs the fetch cycle

conflict_axes.trigger: a clean analogy is memorable but subtly wrong
resolution_order: keep the simplification only if it does not seed a myth
annotate known limits of the analogy
prefer a correct simpler framing over a wrong neat one
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: correctness dominates: a simplification that creates a durable misconception must be replaced
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if no simplification preserves the core truth
conflict_axes.example: 'one character is one byte' as a memorable but false simplification

conflict_axes.trigger: covering many layers shallowly vs one layer deeply for a single question
resolution_order: answer the asked layer deeply enough
link adjacent layers briefly
defer unrelated layers to follow-ups
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: the layer the question targets dominates; adjacent layers get only linking depth
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if the question genuinely spans multiple layers equally
conflict_axes.example: a networking question dragged into full OS scheduling detail

conflict_axes.trigger: Big-O suggests one choice but constants/hardware make another faster at the actual size
resolution_order: state the input-size regime
use Big-O for large n
note constant-factor and cache effects for small n
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for scaling questions Big-O dominates; for fixed small inputs measured/constant-aware reasoning dominates
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if the learner needs a concrete pick at an unstated size
conflict_axes.example: claiming an O(log n) structure is always faster than an O(n) scan

conflict_axes.trigger: cache-friendly contiguous layout vs cheap insertion/deletion or ordered access
resolution_order: identify the dominant operation
pick the structure that optimizes it
explain the conceded tradeoff
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: the dominant operation (random access vs frequent insert vs ordered/keyed lookup) selects the structure
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if the workload mixes operations with no dominant one
conflict_axes.example: using an array for an insert-heavy workload purely for cache reasons

conflict_axes.trigger: spending memory (caching/precompute) to save time vs keeping footprint small
resolution_order: estimate reuse and access cost
cache only when reuse and latency justify it
bound memory growth
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: trade space for time only when reuse and latency gains exceed the memory cost; otherwise keep it small
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if memory is constrained and the gain is uncertain
conflict_axes.example: memoizing results that are never reused and wasting memory

conflict_axes.trigger: exhaustive checking delays delivering a useful answer
resolution_order: verify load-bearing and high-risk claims first
deliver with explicit residual caveats
defer low-value checks
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: correctness of load-bearing claims dominates; remaining low-risk checks may be deferred with disclosure
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if an unverifiable claim is load-bearing
conflict_axes.example: stalling an answer to chase a low-impact citation

conflict_axes.trigger: a canonical text is authoritative but an edition may lag current practice
resolution_order: prefer canonical sources for durable fundamentals
cross-check fast-moving details against current references
flag edition currency
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for stable fundamentals canonical authority dominates; for fast-moving details recency dominates
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if canonical and current sources conflict on a load-bearing fact
conflict_axes.example: citing an old edition for a detail that changed in newer hardware

conflict_axes.trigger: analogies build intuition but can imply false formal guarantees
resolution_order: lead with intuition
state the formal caveat where it changes conclusions
avoid analogies that imply false guarantees
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: intuition leads for literacy, but any formal claim it implies must be verified or hedged
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if an analogy implies a guarantee that is false
conflict_axes.example: an analogy implying NP-hard problems are outright unsolvable

edge_cases.trigger: a concept is placed at the wrong abstraction layer

edge_cases.trigger: explanation asserts one character equals one byte

edge_cases.trigger: explanation claims hash-map lookup is always O(1)
edge_cases.failure_mode: learner ignores worst-case and load-factor degradation
edge_cases.example: asserting guaranteed constant-time membership under adversarial keys
edge_cases.detection_method: flag 'always O(1)' phrasing and require amortized/worst-case wording

edge_cases.trigger: binary search applied to unsorted data
edge_cases.failure_mode: the explanation or example yields wrong results
edge_cases.example: demonstrating binary search on an unsorted array
edge_cases.detection_method: check that any binary-search claim states the sorted precondition

edge_cases.trigger: asymptotic class presented as real-time guarantee
edge_cases.failure_mode: learner picks a worse algorithm for their actual input size

edge_cases.detection_method: check that scaling claims state the input-size regime and constants

edge_cases.trigger: P-vs-NP stated as a settled or absolute result
edge_cases.failure_mode: learner is taught an unsettled question as fact
edge_cases.example: stating NP-hard problems are provably impossible to solve

edge_cases.trigger: recursive example lacks a base case

edge_cases.trigger: a routed source edition is outdated for a fast-moving detail

edge_cases.failure_mode: learner cannot reason about what survives a reboot

edge_cases.trigger: explanation implies adding threads always speeds things up

edge_cases.detection_method: check thread explanations mention races/overhead and bounded speedup

edge_cases.failure_mode: a polished narrative ships an unverified myth

edge_cases.detection_method: check verification gate passed before synthesis lock

acceptance_tests: the chosen layer answers the asked question
goal is correctly read as understanding not build

workflow.objective: map the concept to its layer and adjacent dependencies
acceptance_tests: explanation sits at the targeted layer
relevant adjacent layers are linked

workflow.objective: establish hardware and data-representation foundations the rest depends on
acceptance_tests: overflow/encoding reasoning is correct
memory/storage and latency distinctions hold
workflow.do_first_because: high-coupling foundations (binary, memory) are inherited by software, data-structure, and complexity work-units

workflow.objective: explain the software stack from OS to processes, translation, and networking
acceptance_tests: user/kernel and process/thread distinctions are correct
a web request can be traced end to end

worst-case caveats are present where relevant
exit_criteria: data structures explained with correct cost classes
workflow.do_first_because: data-structure costs are the concrete payoff of the complexity work-units

workflow.objective: explain asymptotic analysis, tractability, recursion, and time/space tradeoffs
acceptance_tests: complexity classes are ordered correctly
tractability and P-vs-NP claims are properly hedged
workflow.do_first_because: complexity vocabulary frames the cost claims made across structures and algorithms

workflow.objective: route each explained concept to authoritative sources at the right depth
acceptance_tests: each concept maps to a named authoritative source
source depth matches the learner goal
workflow.do_first_because: sources must be routed before verification can check claims against them

workflow.objective: verify correctness and flag myths/over-claims before synthesis
acceptance_tests: each claim is checkable against a source

over-claims are removed or flagged

anti_rework_rules.rule: scope the question and target layer before explaining any concept

anti_rework_rules.rule: route authoritative sources before verifying claims
